writing.exampleCaption: The same trait, reached two different ways.
writing.explanation:
A generic bound is resolved at compile time, so the call is direct and inlinable. `dyn Trait` defers the choice to runtime through a vtable, which costs an indirection but lets you store different concrete types together in one collection. A dyn value has no size the compiler can plan for, so it lives behind a pointer: `Box<dyn Trait>` is what goes into a `Vec`.

A trait names behavior that multiple types can provide. `Shape::area` describes what a caller may ask without assuming how a circle or rectangle stores its dimensions. A generic parameter `S: Shape` selects a concrete implementation at compile time; a `&dyn Shape` or `Box<dyn Shape>` selects through a trait object at runtime. Both use the same trait contract, but they solve different API problems.

Use generics when a function can operate on one concrete type per call and compile-time specialization is useful. Use a trait object when a collection must hold values of several concrete types together or when a choice is only known at runtime. Because concrete types can have different sizes, `dyn Shape` is unsized and needs a pointer such as `&dyn Shape` or `Box<dyn Shape>`. The pointer includes enough information to reach the value and its method table. That indirection has a cost, but it can simplify an extensible design.

Try implementing `Shape` for two structs, then call both `a(&shape)` and `b(&shape)` from the example. Put both shapes into a vector of boxed trait objects and sum their areas. Notice the tradeoff: you can call methods exposed by `Shape`, but concrete-only methods are not directly available through the trait object. Write the shared contract at the level callers need, and prefer the simpler generic form unless mixed runtime values are a real requirement.

A trait is most useful when it describes a coherent capability, not simply several methods that happen to be near each other. Keep implementations predictable so generic callers can rely on the contract. When a method needs the concrete `Self` type or a generic parameter, check whether that method should be unavailable through `dyn Trait` or placed in a separate trait.
writing.feedback: A trait object erases the concrete type so the elements share one size.

writing.rule: Generic bound: compile time. dyn Trait: runtime, one indirection.
